etymology: Hebrew Yehoshaphat (H3092) — "Yahweh judges" or "Yahweh has judged." From Yah (the divine name) + shaphat ("to judge, to vindicate").
biblical_def: Jehoshaphat (c. 873 — 849 BC) was the fourth king of the divided southern kingdom of Judah (1 Kings 22:41-50; 2 Chronicles 17-20), son of the reforming king Asa, who reigned twenty-five years and is presented in the canonical record as one of the half-dozen most faithful kings of the Judahite line. His name — "Yahweh judges" — was vindicated in his program of reform: he removed the high places (partly — the record is candid that some remained, 2 Chr 20:33), sent Levites throughout Judah with the book of the law to teach the people (2 Chr 17:7-9 — the first king-led national catechesis in the history of Judah), strengthened the cities and fortified the kingdom, and established a judicial reform in Jerusalem (2 Chr 19:5-11) that anchored the courts in Yahweh's character: "Take heed what ye do: for ye judge not for man, but for the LORD, who is with you in the judgment." His great failure was political-marital: he married his son Jehoram to Athaliah, daughter of Ahab and Jezebel of Israel, an alliance that would nearly destroy the Davidic dynasty within a generation (the Athaliah usurpation, 2 Kings 11). His military narrative includes two great episodes: at Ramoth-Gilead with Ahab (the disastrous joint campaign in which Ahab disguised himself and was killed anyway by an "arrow at a venture," 1 Kings 22), and the Valley of Beracah deliverance (2 Chr 20), where a vast Moabite-Ammonite-Mehunite coalition was destroyed by the LORD himself without Judah lifting a sword — Jehoshaphat's prayer in that chapter ("O our God, wilt thou not judge them? for we have no might against this great company that cometh against us; neither know we what to do: but our eyes are upon thee") is one of the great Old Testament prayers of weakness and faith. The book of Joel later prophesies of the "Valley of Jehoshaphat" (Joel 3:2, 12) as the place of God's final judgment of the nations — eschatological vocabulary built on his name.
webster_summary: Fourth king of Judah (c. 873-849 BC); son of the reforming Asa; reigned 25 years; instituted national catechesis by sending Levites with the book of the law (2 Chr 17); delivered miraculously at the Valley of Beracah (2 Chr 20); name means 'Yahweh judges'.
webster_full: JEHOSHAPHAT, proper noun. Hebrew Yehoshaphat (H3092) — "Yahweh judges" or "Yahweh has judged."
Fourth king of Judah (c. 873-849 BC); son of Asa; reigned 25 years.

Major reform king: removed high places (partially); sent Levites with the book of the law throughout Judah for national catechesis (2 Chr 17:7-9); established judicial reform in Jerusalem (2 Chr 19:5-11).
Famous deliverances: Ramoth-Gilead campaign with Ahab (1 Kings 22), Valley of Beracah miracle (2 Chr 20).
His name lent to the eschatological "Valley of Jehoshaphat" of Joel 3:2, 12.
scriptures: 2 Chronicles 17:7-9

Also in the third year of his reign he sent to his princes... and with them he sent Levites... And they taught in Judah, and had the book of the law of the LORD with them, and went about throughout all the cities of Judah, and taught the people.
2 Chronicles 19:6-7

And [Jehoshaphat] said to the judges, Take heed what ye do: for ye judge not for man, but for the LORD, who is with you in the judgment. Wherefore now let the fear of the LORD be upon you; take heed and do it: for there is no iniquity with the LORD our God, nor respect of persons, nor taking of gifts.
2 Chronicles 20:12
O our God, wilt thou not judge them? for we have no might against this great company that cometh against us; neither know we what to do: but our eyes are upon thee.
Joel 3:12
Let the heathen be wakened, and come up to the valley of Jehoshaphat: for there will I sit to judge all the heathen round about.
corruption_summary: Jehoshaphat is corrupted when his Beracah deliverance is treated as merely a battle-victory rather than as a paradigm of corporate prayer and trust, when his judicial reform is overlooked beside his more dramatic narratives, or when his disastrous marriage-alliance with Ahab is excused on political grounds rather than read as the doctrinal warning Scripture intends.
corruption_paragraphs: Beracah as battle-tactics. The Valley of Beracah deliverance (2 Chr 20) has sometimes been treated as a one-off military miracle — the LORD ambushing the enemy coalition while Judah sang. The chapter itself is constructed as a paradigm: corporate fasting, public prayer of weakness, prophetic word through Jahaziel, worship-as-warfare (Levites singing before the army), trust without sword. The chapter teaches how a Christian people approaches overwhelming adversity, not just how Judah won one battle. Read for the paradigm; do not stop at the tactics.

Ahab-alliance excused as politics. Jehoshaphat married his son Jehoram to Athaliah, Ahab and Jezebel's daughter, almost certainly as a politically calculated north-south alliance to stabilize the divided kingdom against Aramean and Assyrian pressure. The Chronicler refuses the political defense: "shouldest thou help the ungodly, and love them that hate the LORD?" (2 Chr 19:2). The alliance directly produced the Athaliah usurpation (2 Kings 11) and nearly extinguished the Davidic line. The doctrinal lesson is exactly what the Chronicler intended: unequal-yoke alliances with covenant-rejecting partners eventually destroy what they were meant to preserve.
roots_summary: Hebrew Yehoshaphat (H3092) — "Yahweh judges," from Yah (divine name) + shaphat ("to judge"). The fourth king of Judah; his name lent to the eschatological Valley of Jehoshaphat (Joel 3).
roots_lines: Hebrew Yehoshaphat (H3092) — "Yahweh judges" or "Yahweh has judged"
Compound: Yah (the divine name) + shaphat ("to judge, to vindicate, to govern")
Fourth king of the divided southern kingdom of Judah (c. 873-849 BC); son of Asa
Major reform king; introduced national Levitical catechesis (2 Chr 17:7-9); established judicial reform (2 Chr 19)
His name lent to Joel 3:2, 12 "Valley of Jehoshaphat" — the eschatological place of God's judgment of the nations
usage: Jehoshaphat — the reforming king of Judah whose name means 'Yahweh judges'.
Our eyes are upon thee — the Beracah prayer that has become a paradigm of Christian weakness-and-faith.
His marriage-alliance with the house of Ahab is the great warning against unequally-yoked political compromise.

etymology: Hebrew Amatsyahu (H558) — "Yahweh is mighty" or "Yahweh has strength." From amats ("to be strong, to prevail") + Yah (the divine name).
biblical_def: Amaziah (c. 796 — 767 BC) was the ninth king of Judah (2 Kings 14:1-22; 2 Chronicles 25), son of Joash whose own assassination he avenged but whose covenant integrity he could not sustain. Ascended the throne at twenty-five and reigned twenty-nine years — a long reign by Judean standards — but the canonical assessment is mixed: "He did that which was right in the sight of the LORD, yet not with a perfect heart" (2 Chr 25:2). Three episodes define his record. First, the execution of his father's assassins, carried out with deliberate restraint that obeyed Deuteronomy 24:16 ("The fathers shall not be put to death for the children, neither shall the children be put to death for the fathers") and refused the customary ancient-Near-Eastern practice of executing the assassin's children with him (2 Kings 14:5-6) — a striking moment of Mosaic-law fidelity in a small executive matter. Second, his Edomite campaign: hired one hundred thousand Israelite mercenaries from the northern kingdom for a hundred talents of silver, then dismissed them on prophetic counsel and won the Valley of Salt against ten thousand Edomites with Judahite forces alone (2 Chr 25:5-13); but immediately after the victory he brought the captured Edomite gods to Jerusalem and worshiped them — an inexplicable apostasy that the chapter explicitly highlights ("He brought the gods of the children of Seir, and set them up to be his gods, and bowed down himself before them, and burned incense unto them" — 2 Chr 25:14). Third, his ill-fated challenge to King Joash of Israel: pride after the Edomite victory led him to pick a fight he could not win; he was captured, Jerusalem was sacked, and the temple's gold and vessels were carried to Samaria. He was eventually assassinated at Lachish, a fugitive from his own people. His name — "Yahweh is mighty" — was vindicated in his early Edomite victory and indicted by his later worship of the very gods he had defeated.
webster_summary: Ninth king of Judah (c. 796-767 BC); son of Joash; reigned 29 years; executed his father's assassins under Mosaic-law restraint (Deut 24:16); won the Valley of Salt against Edom (2 Chr 25); then worshiped captured Edomite gods and was defeated and humiliated by King Joash of Israel.
webster_full: AMAZIAH, proper noun. Hebrew Amatsyahu (H558) — "Yahweh is mighty," from amats ("to be strong") + Yah.
Ninth king of Judah (c. 796-767 BC); son of Joash; reigned 29 years.

Three signature episodes: principled execution of his father's assassins (2 Kings 14:5-6 / 2 Chr 25:3-4); Valley-of-Salt victory over Edom (2 Chr 25:5-13); apostasy of worshiping captured Edomite gods (2 Chr 25:14) and disastrous war with King Joash of Israel (2 Chr 25:17-24).
Assassinated at Lachish (2 Chr 25:27).
scriptures: 2 Chronicles 25:2
And he did that which was right in the sight of the LORD, but not with a perfect heart.
2 Chronicles 25:14-15

Now it came to pass, after that Amaziah was come from the slaughter of the Edomites, that he brought the gods of the children of Seir, and set them up to be his gods, and bowed down himself before them, and burned incense unto them. Wherefore the anger of the LORD was kindled against Amaziah...
Deuteronomy 24:16
The fathers shall not be put to death for the children, neither shall the children be put to death for the fathers: every man shall be put to death for his own sin.
Proverbs 16:18
Pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall.
corruption_summary: Amaziah is corrupted when his early Deuteronomic restraint with his father's assassins is read as the totality of his record without the later apostasy that defined his reign, when the absurd Edomite-gods episode is treated as merely strange without the doctrinal weight Scripture gives it, or when the Israelite-mercenary dismissal is read tactically rather than as obedience to a prophet's word.
corruption_paragraphs: Selective-virtue reading. Some readings of Amaziah lift the Deuteronomy-24:16 restraint with his father's assassins as evidence of his deep Mosaic-law obedience. The chapter as a whole resists this selective lift: the same king who refused to kill children for their fathers' crimes brought enemy gods home and worshiped them, then went to war out of pride and lost his kingdom's wealth. The verse-by-verse Mosaic-law detail in one matter is not equivalent to wholehearted obedience in the rest of life. The Chronicler's summary verdict ("right in the sight of the LORD, yet not with a perfect heart") refuses the selective virtue.

Edomite-gods absurdity. The episode in 2 Chr 25:14 — bringing the gods of a people he had just defeated and worshiping them — is so theologically absurd that some modern readers treat it as embellishment. The Chronicler's prophet (anonymous) recognized the absurdity in real time and asked the king bluntly: "Why hast thou sought after the gods of the people, which could not deliver their own people out of thine hand?" (2 Chr 25:15). The Chronicler is making a doctrinal point about idolatry: it is not rational; it is the heart's foolishness, defended even against the obvious failure of the false god to save its own people.
roots_summary: Hebrew Amatsyahu (H558) — "Yahweh is mighty," from amats + Yah. The ninth king of Judah; son of Joash; reigned 29 years.
roots_lines: Hebrew Amatsyahu (H558) — "Yahweh is mighty" or "Yahweh has strength"
Compound: amats ("to be strong, to prevail") + Yah (the divine name)
Ninth king of the divided southern kingdom of Judah (c. 796-767 BC)
Son of Joash; father of Uzziah/Azariah (his successor)
Two main accounts: 2 Kings 14:1-22 (briefer) and 2 Chronicles 25 (fuller)
usage: Amaziah — "Yahweh is mighty"; the ninth king of Judah who started with Deuteronomic restraint and ended worshiping captured Edomite gods.
Right in the sight of the LORD, yet not with a perfect heart — the Chronicler's summary verdict.
His career is a sustained meditation on the difference between partial obedience and wholehearted covenant fidelity.

etymology: Hebrew Yotham (H3147) — "Yahweh is perfect/complete" or possibly "the LORD is upright." From Yah (the divine name) + tam ("perfect, complete, blameless").
biblical_def: Jotham (c. 750 — 735 BC) was the eleventh king of Judah (2 Kings 15:32-38; 2 Chronicles 27), son of the leprous king Uzziah/Azariah, contemporary of the prophets Isaiah, Hosea, and Micah whose ministries opened during his reign. Sixteen-year reign according to the canonical accession formula. He is one of only four Judahite kings the Chronicler can describe without qualification as having done right in the sight of the LORD (the others being Asa, Hezekiah, and Josiah) — though even this praise is followed by the standard note that the high places were not removed (2 Kings 15:35). His name — "Yahweh is perfect" — was reflected in his personal integrity: "So Jotham became mighty, because he prepared his ways before the LORD his God" (2 Chr 27:6). His public record is light by Chronicler standards: he built the upper gate of the temple, fortified the walls of Ophel, and successfully campaigned against the Ammonites who paid him a hundred talents of silver, ten thousand measures of wheat, and ten thousand of barley for three years running (2 Chr 27:5). The most theologically striking detail is the Chronicler's observation in 2 Chr 27:2: he did right "howbeit he entered not into the temple of the LORD" — a deliberate reverent restraint after his father Uzziah was struck with leprosy for entering the temple to offer incense (2 Chr 26:16-21). Jotham learned the lesson his father had to be struck with leprosy to learn: priestly and kingly offices are distinct and the king does not invade priestly territory. The Isaiah, Hosea, and Micah prophecies dated to Jotham's reign give us his most enduring legacy: under a faithful but quiet king the great writing prophets of the eighth century began the public ministry that would shape Old Testament canon and call Judah toward and beyond the exile.
webster_summary: Eleventh king of Judah (c. 750-735 BC); son of leprous Uzziah; reigned 16 years; one of only four Judahite kings the Chronicler can call wholly faithful (with Asa, Hezekiah, Josiah); contemporary of Isaiah, Hosea, and Micah whose prophetic ministries began under him.
webster_full: JOTHAM, proper noun. Hebrew Yotham (H3147) — "Yahweh is perfect/complete," from Yah + tam.
Eleventh king of the divided southern kingdom of Judah (c. 750-735 BC); son of the leprous king Uzziah (Azariah); father of the wicked Ahaz.
Reigned 16 years; one of only four Judahite kings called wholly faithful by the Chronicler (with Asa, Hezekiah, Josiah).
Built the upper gate of the temple, fortified the wall of Ophel, subdued the Ammonites; "entered not into the temple of the LORD" out of reverent restraint (2 Chr 27:2).
Contemporary of Isaiah, Hosea, and Micah whose canonical prophetic ministries began during his reign.
scriptures: 2 Chronicles 27:6
So Jotham became mighty, because he prepared his ways before the LORD his God.
2 Chronicles 27:2
And he did that which was right in the sight of the LORD, according to all that his father Uzziah did: howbeit he entered not into the temple of the LORD. And the people did yet corruptly.
Isaiah 1:1
The vision of Isaiah the son of Amoz, which he saw concerning Judah and Jerusalem in the days of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah.
Micah 1:1
The word of the LORD that came to Micah the Morasthite in the days of Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah.
corruption_summary: Jotham is corrupted when his quiet faithfulness is overlooked in favor of his more dramatic predecessors and successors, when his "entered not into the temple" restraint is treated as a footnote rather than as a deliberate Chronicler-emphasized lesson learned from his father's leprosy, or when the prophets of his reign are read in isolation from the kingly context the Chronicler carefully preserves.
corruption_paragraphs: Quiet-king neglect. Sandwiched between his more dramatic father (Uzziah's leprosy) and his more dramatic son (Ahaz's apostasy), Jotham receives only twelve verses of attention in 2 Kings 15:32-38 and a modest chapter in 2 Chronicles 27. Many readers skip him. But the Chronicler signals his importance by giving him the wholly-faithful designation (with Asa, Hezekiah, and Josiah) and the rare unqualified verdict of his strength deriving from his prepared ways. The lesson is doctrinal: quiet faithfulness is not less worthy of canonical attention than dramatic apostasy or reform. The Chronicler models the discipline of seeing it.

Temple-restraint underestimated. 2 Chr 27:2's note that Jotham did right "howbeit he entered not into the temple of the LORD" is rendered in many translations and read by many readers as a passing remark. The Chronicler intended it as a key explanatory contrast with his father: Uzziah had entered the temple to offer incense and was struck with leprosy on the spot (2 Chr 26:16-21). Jotham, watching his father live the last years of his reign in a separate house as a leper, learned the lesson. The restraint is not a footnote; it is a son refusing the office-confusion that destroyed his father.
roots_summary: Hebrew Yotham (H3147) — "Yahweh is perfect/complete," from Yah + tam. The eleventh king of Judah (c. 750-735 BC); son of leprous Uzziah; contemporary of Isaiah, Hosea, Micah.
roots_lines: Hebrew Yotham (H3147) — "Yahweh is perfect" or "Yahweh is complete/upright"
Compound: Yah (the divine name) + tam ("perfect, complete, blameless")
Eleventh king of the divided southern kingdom of Judah (c. 750-735 BC)
Son of the leprous Uzziah/Azariah; father of the apostate Ahaz
Contemporary of Isaiah (Isa 1:1), Hosea (Hos 1:1), and Micah (Mic 1:1) whose canonical prophetic ministries began under him
usage: Jotham — "Yahweh is perfect"; the quietly faithful eleventh king of Judah.
He prepared his ways before the LORD his God (2 Chr 27:6) — the explanation of his strength.
Sandwiched between his dramatic father (Uzziah-the-leper) and his apostate son (Ahaz); under his reign the great eighth-century prophets began canonical ministry.

etymology: Hebrew Achaz (H271) — "he has grasped" or "possessor"; a shortened form of Yehoachaz, "Yahweh has grasped" (which is the form preserved in 2 Chronicles 28 in some manuscripts). The same root produced the Assyrian-tablet name Yauhazi (the form by which Tiglath-Pileser III recorded him in his royal annals).
biblical_def: Ahaz (c. 735 — 715 BC) was the twelfth king of Judah (2 Kings 16; 2 Chronicles 28; Isaiah 7), son of the faithful Jotham, whose sixteen-year reign produced the deepest apostasy in pre-exilic Judahite history before Manasseh and whose famous interview with the prophet Isaiah produced the most theologically loaded sign-prophecy in the Old Testament (Isa 7:14, the Immanuel prophecy). Ahaz reigned during the great Syro-Ephraimite crisis (c. 734-732 BC), when Rezin king of Aram and Pekah king of Israel allied to depose him and replace him with a puppet ("the son of Tabeel," Isa 7:6), planning to detach Judah from any Assyrian-loyalty axis. Isaiah confronted him at the conduit of the upper pool with a two-fold word: do not fear these two smoking firebrands (Isa 7:4) and ask the LORD for any sign in heaven or earth to confirm the promise (Isa 7:10-12). Ahaz famously refused the sign with sham-piety: "I will not ask, neither will I tempt the LORD." Isaiah then gave the sign anyway: "Therefore the Lord himself shall give you a sign; Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel" (Isa 7:14) — the prophecy Matthew 1:23 applies to the virgin birth of Christ. Ahaz refused the sign and made his own political solution: he stripped the temple and palace treasuries to bribe Tiglath-Pileser III of Assyria to attack Damascus and Israel for him (2 Kings 16:7-9). Tiglath-Pileser obliged but extracted from Ahaz a vassal-treaty that put Judah under permanent Assyrian tribute. Ahaz further apostatized: he saw an altar at Damascus he admired, sent its measurements home to the priest Urijah, who built a copy in the Jerusalem temple before Ahaz returned; Ahaz then offered on the new altar and moved the bronze altar of Yahweh aside (2 Kings 16:10-16). He shut up the doors of the temple of the LORD entirely toward the end of his reign (2 Chr 28:24), built high places "in every several city of Judah," and burned his own sons in the fire to Molech in the Valley of Hinnom (2 Chr 28:3).
webster_summary: Twelfth king of Judah (c. 735-715 BC); son of the faithful Jotham; the Immanuel-prophecy recipient (Isa 7:14) who refused the sign offered by Isaiah; bribed Tiglath-Pileser III of Assyria; built a Damascene altar in the temple; burned his own sons to Molech; shut the temple doors.
webster_full: AHAZ, proper noun. Hebrew Achaz (H271) — "he has grasped" (shortened from Yehoachaz, "Yahweh has grasped").
Twelfth king of Judah (c. 735-715 BC); son of Jotham; father of Hezekiah.
Reigned during the Syro-Ephraimite crisis (c. 734-732 BC); recipient of Isaiah's Immanuel prophecy (Isa 7:14) which he refused as a sign.

Bribed Tiglath-Pileser III of Assyria to attack Damascus and Israel (2 Kings 16:7-9); built a Damascene-pattern altar in the Jerusalem temple; sacrificed his own sons in the fire to Molech (2 Chr 28:3); shut the doors of the temple (2 Chr 28:24).
Appears in Assyrian royal annals as Yauhazi.
scriptures: Isaiah 7:9
If ye will not believe, surely ye shall not be established.
Isaiah 7:14
Therefore the Lord himself shall give you a sign; Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel.
2 Chronicles 28:3
Moreover [Ahaz] burnt incense in the valley of the son of Hinnom, and burnt his children in the fire, after the abominations of the heathen whom the LORD had cast out before the children of Israel.
2 Kings 16:7-8

So Ahaz sent messengers to Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria, saying, I am thy servant and thy son... And Ahaz took the silver and gold that was found in the house of the LORD, and in the treasures of the king's house, and sent it for a present to the king of Assyria.
corruption_summary: Ahaz is corrupted when his refusal of Isaiah's sign is read as humble piety rather than as the deliberate evasion Isaiah immediately condemned, when the Immanuel prophecy is detached from the historical setting that gave it weight, or when his vassalage to Tiglath-Pileser is excused as political necessity rather than read as the covenant-betrayal Scripture intends.
corruption_paragraphs: Sham-piety refusal misread. "I will not ask, neither will I tempt the LORD" sounds reverent until one reads the next verse: "And [Isaiah] said, Hear ye now, O house of David; Is it a small thing for you to weary men, but will ye weary my God also? Therefore the Lord himself shall give you a sign" (Isa 7:13-14). Isaiah saw through it instantly: this was not piety, it was unbelief dressed up in pious-sounding refusal because Ahaz had already decided to bribe Tiglath-Pileser and did not want a Yahweh-sign that would have committed him to trust the LORD instead. The reader should hear Isaiah's pastoral exasperation in 7:13.

Political-necessity excuse. Modern readings sometimes treat Ahaz's appeal to Assyria as understandable real-politik: faced with the Syro-Ephraimite alliance threatening to depose him, what choice did he have but to call on the only superpower available? The text rejects this defense. Isaiah explicitly offered him an alternative: trust the LORD's word about the Syro-Ephraimite threat (Isa 7:4-9). Ahaz refused not because no alternative existed but because trust-in-Yahweh was the alternative he refused. The wages of his refusal: a hundred years of Assyrian vassalage, the eventual fall of Israel (722 BC), and the near-fall of Judah (Sennacherib at the gates in 701).
roots_summary: Hebrew Achaz (H271) — "he has grasped," from achaz ("to grasp, take hold"). Shortened from Yehoachaz, "Yahweh has grasped." Twelfth king of Judah (c. 735-715 BC).
roots_lines: Hebrew Achaz (H271) — "he has grasped, possessor"; from achaz ("to grasp, take hold")
Shortened form of Yehoachaz — "Yahweh has grasped"; the longer form appears in Assyrian sources as Yauhazi
Twelfth king of the divided southern kingdom of Judah (c. 735-715 BC)
Son of Jotham; father of Hezekiah
Recipient of Isaiah's Immanuel prophecy at the upper-pool conduit (Isa 7:1-25); the New Testament cites Isa 7:14 of the virgin birth (Matt 1:23)
usage: Ahaz — the apostate twelfth king of Judah who refused Isaiah's offered sign.
If ye will not believe, surely ye shall not be established (Isa 7:9) — the prophetic warning he ignored.
Father of Hezekiah; the deepest apostate before Manasseh; the king to whom the Immanuel prophecy was first delivered.

etymology: Hebrew Amon (H526) — possibly "skilled workman" (from aman, "to nurture, support, be faithful") or "hidden" (cognate with the Egyptian god Amun, whom his idolatrous father Manasseh may have honored in naming him). The Hebrew root produces both amen ("truly, faithful") and omanut ("craftsmanship"); the ambiguity of the king's name is itself a small commentary on his confused inheritance.
biblical_def: Amon (c. 642 — 640 BC) was the fifteenth king of Judah (2 Kings 21:19-26; 2 Chronicles 33:21-25), son of the deeply apostate Manasseh, father of the great reformer Josiah, whose two-year reign was so brief and so wicked that the canonical record dispatches him in less than half a chapter in each account. Twenty-two years old at his accession; reigned two years; assassinated by his own servants in his palace at age twenty-four. The Chronicler's verdict is unsparing: "he did that which was evil in the sight of the LORD, as did Manasseh his father: for Amon sacrificed unto all the carved images which Manasseh his father had made, and served them; And humbled not himself before the LORD, as Manasseh his father had humbled himself; but Amon trespassed more and more" (2 Chr 33:22-23). The phrase "trespassed more and more" sets him below his father: Manasseh had at least repented at the end of his long reign in Assyrian captivity (2 Chr 33:12-13), but Amon refused that humbling and continued the idolatry without the late-life remorse. His assassination is recorded without dynastic crisis: the people of Judah killed his assassins and made his eight-year-old son Josiah king in his place, an extraordinary popular intervention that preserved the Davidic line through the boy who would become the greatest reform-king of the divided monarchy. The Chronicler's silence on Amon's burial (he was buried in the garden of Uzza, his father's burial place, 2 Kings 21:26, rather than in the royal tombs) is itself a final commentary. The two-year reign is one of the shortest in the canonical record; the assassination one of the few palace coups in Davidic-Judah history; the popular intervention to install Josiah one of the most extraordinary moments of divine providence preserving the Davidic line.
webster_summary: Fifteenth king of Judah (c. 642-640 BC); son of Manasseh; father of Josiah; reigned only 2 years; assassinated by his own servants; the Chronicler's verdict: 'trespassed more and more' (refused the late-life humbling that even his father Manasseh had received).
webster_full: AMON, proper noun. Hebrew Amon (H526) — possibly "skilled workman" (from aman) or echoing the Egyptian god name. Distinct from Ammon (a different Hebrew name and the related people group).
Fifteenth king of Judah (c. 642-640 BC); son of Manasseh; father of Josiah.
Reigned only 2 years; assassinated by his own servants in the palace; the people then killed the assassins and made his eight-year-old son Josiah king.
Verdict: 'did evil in the sight of the LORD as did Manasseh his father... humbled not himself... trespassed more and more' (2 Chr 33:22-23).
scriptures: 2 Chronicles 33:22-23

But [Amon] did that which was evil in the sight of the LORD, as did Manasseh his father: for Amon sacrificed unto all the carved images which Manasseh his father had made, and served them; And humbled not himself before the LORD, as Manasseh his father had humbled himself; but Amon trespassed more and more.

And the servants of Amon conspired against him, and slew the king in his own house. And the people of the land slew all them that had conspired against king Amon; and the people of the land made Josiah his son king in his stead.
Zephaniah 1:1
The word of the LORD which came unto Zephaniah... in the days of Josiah the son of Amon, king of Judah.
Matthew 1:10
And Ezekias begat Manasses; and Manasses begat Amon; and Amon begat Josias.
corruption_summary: Amon is corrupted when his short wicked reign is treated as merely an interlude between Manasseh's drama and Josiah's reform rather than as a serious doctrinal warning about generational reception of repentance, when his refusal of his father's late-life humbling is overlooked, or when the popular intervention to install Josiah is treated as political accident rather than divine providence.
corruption_paragraphs: Interlude misreading. Amon's two-year reign and assassination are often skipped in popular Bible reading: a wicked father (Manasseh), a wicked son (Amon), and then the great reformer Josiah. The Chronicler's careful theological framing resists this skip. Amon was offered the same Yahweh that his father had finally come to in Assyrian captivity; Amon refused. The verdict 'humbled not himself, as Manasseh his father had humbled himself; but Amon trespassed more and more' (2 Chr 33:23) means the son had access to his father's late-life testimony and turned away from it. The doctrinal lesson is generational and severe: each generation must receive the gospel personally; no son is automatically saved by his father's eventual repentance.

Popular-intervention as accident. The episode in 2 Kings 21:24 and 2 Chr 33:25 — the people of the land killing Amon's assassins and installing his eight-year-old son Josiah — is not a colorful political vignette. The Chronicler is making a theological point: the LORD preserved the Davidic line through popular intervention against a coup that could easily have ended the dynasty. Eight-year-old Josiah survived because Judah's covenant-people refused to accept a non-Davidic king. The text is celebrating the LORD's faithfulness to 2 Samuel 7:16 through the agency of the people of the land.
roots_summary: Hebrew Amon (H526) — possibly "skilled workman" (from aman, "to nurture, support") or echoing the Egyptian god Amun. Fifteenth king of Judah (c. 642-640 BC); two-year reign; assassinated.
roots_lines: Hebrew Amon (H526) — possibly "skilled workman" or "hidden" (cognate with Egyptian god Amun)
From the root aman ("to nurture, support, be faithful") — same root that produces amen
Distinct from Ammon (H5983), the people-group descended from Lot
Fifteenth king of the divided southern kingdom of Judah (c. 642-640 BC)

usage: Amon — the fifteenth king of Judah; son of Manasseh; father of Josiah; assassinated after a 2-year reign.
Trespassed more and more — the Chronicler's verdict; he refused the humbling that even his father had finally accepted.
The popular installation of his eight-year-old son Josiah preserved the Davidic line by divine providence through the people of the land.

etymology: Hebrew Omri (H6018) — possibly "life" or "servant of Yahweh"; uncertain. The Assyrian and Moabite inscriptions transliterate the name Humri or Khumri, and for centuries afterward the Assyrian royal annals referred to the northern kingdom as "the house of Omri" (Bit-Humri) even after his dynasty had fallen — testimony to his political-military weight in international affairs.
biblical_def: Omri (c. 885 — 874 BC) was the sixth king of the northern kingdom of Israel (1 Kings 16:15-28), founder of the Omride dynasty, builder of the capital city of Samaria, father of the notorious Ahab, and one of the most internationally significant kings of the divided monarchy — almost universally treated in extrabiblical Assyrian and Moabite sources but dispatched in only fourteen verses by the canonical record because his doctrinal record was so wicked. He rose to power as a military commander when his predecessor Zimri assassinated King Elah and seized the throne for seven days (1 Kings 16:9-15); the army at Gibbethon proclaimed Omri king instead, who marched on Tirzah, took the city, and watched Zimri burn the palace down around himself rather than be captured. For four years thereafter Omri fought a civil war against a rival claimant, Tibni son of Ginath, finally prevailing in the field. He then made the political-geographic decision that defined the remaining history of the northern kingdom: he bought the hill of Shomron (Samaria) from a man named Shemer for two talents of silver and built a new capital there (1 Kings 16:24). Samaria became the seat of Israel's monarchy until its fall to Assyria in 722 BC, and the name passed to the surrounding region ("the country of the Samaritans") and to the post-exilic Samaritans of New Testament times (John 4). The canonical verdict is severe: "Omri wrought evil in the eyes of the LORD, and did worse than all that were before him" (1 Kings 16:25). His son Ahab and grandson Joram continued the dynasty in the same wicked pattern; his daughter Athaliah carried the Omride apostasy south by marriage into the Davidic house and almost destroyed it. Micah 6:16 specifically denounces "the statutes of Omri" as a continuing snare to Israel a century after his death.
webster_summary: Sixth king of the northern kingdom of Israel (c. 885-874 BC); founder of the Omride dynasty; built the capital of Samaria; father of Ahab; called 'worse than all that were before him' (1 Kings 16:25); the international Assyrian annals continued to call Israel 'the house of Omri' for centuries.
webster_full: OMRI, proper noun. Hebrew Omri (H6018); uncertain meaning; possibly "life" or "servant of Yahweh." Assyrian and Moabite sources transliterate Humri/Khumri.
Sixth king of the divided northern kingdom of Israel (c. 885-874 BC); founder of the Omride dynasty.
Built the capital city of Samaria on a hill bought from Shemer for two talents of silver (1 Kings 16:24); the city remained Israel's capital until 722 BC.
Father of Ahab; grandfather of Joram; great-uncle (through Athaliah's marriage to Jehoram of Judah) of the Judahite Ahaziah; the Omride dynasty's apostasy poisoned both kingdoms for a generation.
Mentioned in extrabiblical sources: Mesha Stele (Moabite), Black Obelisk of Shalmaneser III (Assyrian), royal annals of Tiglath-Pileser III (Assyrian).
scriptures: In the thirty and first year of Asa king of Judah began Omri to reign over Israel, twelve years: six years reigned he in Tirzah. And he bought the hill Samaria of Shemer for two talents of silver, and built on the hill, and called the name of the city which he built, after the name of Shemer, owner of the hill, Samaria.
But Omri wrought evil in the eyes of the LORD, and did worse than all that were before him. For he walked in all the way of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, and in his sin wherewith he made Israel to sin.
Micah 6:16
For the statutes of Omri are kept, and all the works of the house of Ahab, and ye walk in their counsels; that I should make thee a desolation, and the inhabitants thereof an hissing.
Joshua 13:1-2
Now Joshua was old and stricken in years; and the LORD said unto him, Thou art old and stricken in years, and there remaineth yet very much land to be possessed.
corruption_summary: Omri is corrupted when his international political-military significance is read as positive achievement rather than as canon's deliberately understated record of a wicked king, when the building of Samaria is treated as urban-planning success rather than as the symbol of northern apostasy it became, or when his statutes (Mic 6:16) are read merely historically without their continuing covenant-warning weight.
corruption_paragraphs: Political-success-as-canonical-praise. Omri was clearly successful by the metrics of ancient Near Eastern statecraft: he ended a civil war, founded a long-lived capital city, established a dynasty that lasted three generations (until Jehu's coup), and made the northern kingdom internationally consequential enough that Assyria continued to refer to Israel as 'the house of Omri' for two centuries after his death. The canonical record allots him fourteen verses and a damning verdict. Modern Near-Eastern-history readings sometimes flip this proportion and treat the Bible's reticence as a curious gap. The Chronicler's logic is theological: political success without covenant fidelity is not worth more space; the LORD's people need to know that Omri did worse than all before him, not how many talents of silver he weighed out for Samaria.

Mesha-Stele-tourism. The Moabite king Mesha's stele (discovered 1868) gives a Moabite account of struggling against Omri and Ahab that has fascinated archaeologists for over a century. Some treatments lift this archaeological celebrity into a positive Omri rehabilitation: he must have been an impressive king if Mesha had to fight him so hard. The stele is genuinely interesting as confirmation of biblical narrative; it does not change the canonical verdict. The doctrinal point about Omri is unchanged by the size of the army Moab had to raise to resist him: he led Israel in the way of Jeroboam son of Nebat, and the LORD's witness against him stands.
roots_summary: Hebrew Omri (H6018); uncertain meaning, possibly "life" or "servant of Yahweh." Sixth king of Israel (c. 885-874 BC); founder of the Omride dynasty; builder of Samaria.

usage: Omri — the sixth king of Israel; founder of the Omride dynasty; builder of Samaria.
Worse than all that were before him (1 Kings 16:25); his name in Assyrian sources outlasted his dynasty.
His daughter Athaliah carried the Omride apostasy south by marriage into the Davidic house and almost destroyed it.

etymology: Hebrew Athalyah (H6271) — possibly "Yahweh is exalted" or "Yahweh has constrained"; uncertain. The Yahwistic ending is striking on a queen who actively worked to extinguish Yahwistic worship in Judah; ancient Near Eastern theophoric names often outlived the religious commitments they originally signaled.
biblical_def: Athaliah (c. 841 — 835 BC) was the only queen regnant in the history of the divided southern kingdom of Judah (2 Kings 11; 2 Chronicles 22:10-23:21), daughter of Omri and Ahab of Israel and granddaughter of Jezebel, who married Jehoram king of Judah (the son of the faithful Jehoshaphat) and brought the Omride apostasy with her into the Davidic house. When her husband Jehoram died and her son Ahaziah of Judah was killed by Jehu's revolt in Israel (2 Kings 9:27), Athaliah seized power in Jerusalem by murdering every member of the Davidic royal family she could find — her own grandsons — in a comprehensive dynastic massacre intended to extinguish the line of David and replace it with the Omride dynasty extending into Judah. Only the infant Joash escaped, hidden by his aunt Jehosheba (the wife of the high priest Jehoiada) for six years in the temple while Athaliah reigned as queen. The episode is one of the most extraordinary in Scripture: the Davidic covenant of 2 Samuel 7:16 ("thine house and thy kingdom shall be established for ever before thee: thy throne shall be established for ever") came perilously close to extinction through a single hand, the hand of Jezebel's daughter. In the seventh year of Athaliah's reign (835 BC) Jehoiada the high priest organized a coordinated coup: the Levitical guard formed a protective ring around the boy-king Joash, the elders crowned him in the temple, the people of Judah shouted "God save the king," and Athaliah was led out from the temple precinct (so as not to defile it with her blood) and killed at the horse-gate of the palace. Her seven-year usurpation is the only break in the unbroken Davidic line from David to Zedekiah, and the Davidic covenant survived only by the courage of the high priest's wife and the providence of the LORD over the one infant who escaped.
webster_summary: Only queen regnant of Judah (c. 841-835 BC); daughter of Ahab and Jezebel of Israel; married Jehoram of Judah; murdered her own Davidic grandsons to seize the throne; reigned 7 years; deposed by the high priest Jehoiada's coup that installed the boy-king Joash; killed at the horse-gate.
webster_full: ATHALIAH, proper noun. Hebrew Athalyah (H6271); uncertain meaning; possibly "Yahweh is exalted" or "Yahweh has constrained."
Daughter of Ahab and Jezebel of Israel (or, by some readings, of Omri); married Jehoram king of Judah, son of the faithful Jehoshaphat.
After her son Ahaziah of Judah was killed in Jehu's revolt (2 Kings 9:27), she murdered every Davidic royal she could find and reigned as queen regnant of Judah for 7 years (c. 841-835 BC).
Only the infant Joash escaped, hidden in the temple by his aunt Jehosheba (wife of the high priest Jehoiada).
Deposed by Jehoiada's coordinated coup at the temple; killed at the horse-gate of the palace (2 Kings 11:16).
scriptures: 2 Kings 11:1-3

And when Athaliah the mother of Ahaziah saw that her son was dead, she arose and destroyed all the seed royal. But Jehosheba, the daughter of king Joram, sister of Ahaziah, took Joash the son of Ahaziah, and stole him from among the king's sons which were slain; and they hid him, even him and his nurse, in the bedchamber from Athaliah, so that he was not slain. And he was with her hid in the house of the LORD six years. And Athaliah did reign over the land.
2 Samuel 7:16
And thine house and thy kingdom shall be established for ever before thee: thy throne shall be established for ever.
2 Chronicles 22:10-11

But when Athaliah the mother of Ahaziah saw that her son was dead, she arose and destroyed all the seed royal of the house of Judah. But Jehoshabeath, the daughter of the king, took Joash the son of Ahaziah, and stole him from among the king's sons that were slain, and put him and his nurse in a bedchamber. So Jehoshabeath, the daughter of king Jehoram, the wife of Jehoiada the priest...

Nevertheless my lovingkindness will I not utterly take from him, nor suffer my faithfulness to fail. My covenant will I not break, nor alter the thing that is gone out of my lips. Once have I sworn by my holiness that I will not lie unto David. His seed shall endure for ever, and his throne as the sun before me.
corruption_summary: Athaliah is corrupted when her queenship is read through modern feminist lenses as merely a queen who happened to be evil rather than as the deliberate Omride-dynastic invasion of the Davidic line, when her seven-year reign is treated as a curiosity rather than as the moment the Davidic covenant nearly failed, or when Jehosheba's quiet heroism is overlooked beside the more dramatic Jehoiada-coup.
corruption_paragraphs: Female-monarch-as-modern-cause. Some contemporary readings present Athaliah as an early example of female political agency — a woman who took power, ruled, and was killed. The text refuses this framing. The chapters resist any sympathetic reading of Athaliah: she is depicted as the granddaughter of Jezebel completing what her grandmother began, murdering her own Davidic grandsons to extinguish the line of David, and ruling Judah on Omride-pagan principles while the rightful king hid in the temple. The text's interest is not in her gender but in her covenant-treason against the Davidic dynasty her mother-in-law had been brought into to corrupt.

Jehosheba-overlooked. Jehoiada the high priest gets named more often in the narrative, but the woman who actually preserved the Davidic line was Jehosheba (also spelled Jehoshabeath), Jehoram's daughter and Joash's aunt and Jehoiada's wife. While Athaliah was systematically killing the royal children, Jehosheba slipped the infant Joash out of the slaughter and hid him with his nurse in the temple bedchamber for six years. The Davidic covenant survived through a high-priest's wife who refused to let the line of David die. The text honors her by naming her in both 2 Kings 11:2 and 2 Chr 22:11.
roots_summary: Hebrew Athalyah (H6271); uncertain meaning, possibly "Yahweh is exalted." The only queen regnant of Judah (c. 841-835 BC); daughter of Ahab and Jezebel; usurped after Davidic massacre; deposed by Jehoiada.

Daughter of Ahab and Jezebel of Israel; granddaughter of Omri
Married Jehoram king of Judah, son of the faithful Jehoshaphat; mother of Ahaziah of Judah
After her son was killed in Jehu's revolt (841 BC), she murdered the Davidic royal family and reigned as queen 7 years (c. 841-835 BC)
The infant Joash, her grandson, was hidden in the temple by her sister-in-law Jehosheba and his nurse for the duration of her reign
usage: Athaliah — the only queen regnant of Judah; daughter of Ahab and Jezebel; nearly extinguished the Davidic line.
Hidden in the house of the LORD six years — the seven-year suspension of the Davidic line, broken by the courage of Jehosheba.
The Davidic covenant of 2 Samuel 7:16 was tested most severely under her usurpation; the one infant who survived became the king Joash.

etymology: Hebrew Hoshea (H1954) — "salvation" or "he has saved"; from yasha ("to save, deliver"). The same root produces both the Hebrew name and (with the Yah- prefix) the name Yehoshua — "Yahweh saves," rendered into Greek as Iēsous, "Jesus." Moses's original name for his successor Joshua was Hoshea (Num 13:8), which Moses then expanded to Joshua (Num 13:16).
biblical_def: Hoshea (c. 732 — 722 BC) was the nineteenth and final king of the divided northern kingdom of Israel (2 Kings 17:1-23), assassin of his predecessor Pekah, vassal of the Assyrian kings Tiglath-Pileser III and Shalmaneser V, and the king during whose reign Samaria fell to Sargon II of Assyria in 722 BC and the ten northern tribes were carried into the captivity from which they never returned as a distinct people. His nine-year reign represents the slow strangulation of the northern kingdom by Assyrian power. The canonical verdict is striking: "And he did that which was evil in the sight of the LORD, but not as the kings of Israel that were before him" (2 Kings 17:2) — the only Israelite king of whom the not-as-bad-as-his-predecessors qualifier is used. The Chronicler does not narrate his reign at all (he focuses entirely on the southern kingdom by this point). His name — "salvation" — is haunting: he was the final king and his name meant deliverance, but no deliverance came. He attempted to break free from Assyrian vassalage by appealing for help to So king of Egypt (probably Osorkon IV or possibly Tefnakht of Sais); Shalmaneser V detected the rebellion, imprisoned Hoshea, besieged Samaria for three years (725-722 BC), and finally took the city. The 27 verses of 2 Kings 17:7-23 constitute the most sustained Old Testament theological retrospective on why the northern kingdom fell: idolatry from the days of Jeroboam I, refusal of prophetic warning, golden calves at Bethel and Dan, high places, asherah-poles, child-sacrifice, Baal-worship, divination, and ultimately exile. The chapter is essential reading for understanding the structure of covenant judgment in the divided monarchy.
webster_summary: Nineteenth and final king of the northern kingdom of Israel (c. 732-722 BC); vassal of Assyria; rebelled by appealing to Egypt; Samaria fell to Sargon II in 722 BC and the ten tribes were carried into exile; called 'evil but not as the kings of Israel before him' (2 Kings 17:2).
webster_full: HOSHEA, proper noun. Hebrew Hoshea (H1954) — "salvation," from yasha ("to save"). Same root as Joshua (Yehoshua, "Yahweh saves") and ultimately Jesus.
Nineteenth and final king of the divided northern kingdom of Israel (c. 732-722 BC); assassinated Pekah to take the throne (2 Kings 15:30).
Vassal of Tiglath-Pileser III and Shalmaneser V; rebelled by appealing to So king of Egypt; imprisoned by Shalmaneser; Samaria besieged 725-722 BC.
Samaria fell to Sargon II of Assyria in 722 BC; the ten northern tribes carried into Assyrian exile.
Distinct from Hosea the prophet (same Hebrew name but different person; Hos 1:1).
scriptures: 2 Kings 17:2-4

And he did that which was evil in the sight of the LORD, but not as the kings of Israel that were before him. Against him came up Shalmaneser king of Assyria; and Hoshea became his servant, and gave him presents. And the king of Assyria found conspiracy in Hoshea: for he had sent messengers to So king of Egypt, and brought no present to the king of Assyria, as he had done year by year: therefore the king of Assyria shut him up, and bound him in prison.
2 Kings 17:6
In the ninth year of Hoshea the king of Assyria took Samaria, and carried Israel away into Assyria, and placed them in Halah and in Habor by the river of Gozan, and in the cities of the Medes.
2 Kings 17:18
Therefore the LORD was very angry with Israel, and removed them out of his sight: there was none left but the tribe of Judah only.
Hosea 13:16
Samaria shall become desolate; for she hath rebelled against her God: they shall fall by the sword: their infants shall be dashed in pieces, and their women with child shall be ripped up.
corruption_summary: Hoshea is corrupted when the 'evil but not as the kings before him' qualifier is read as partial vindication rather than as the bitter Chronicler-irony it actually is, when his fall is treated as merely the outcome of geopolitical pressure rather than as covenant judgment, or when the 27-verse theological retrospective of 2 Kings 17:7-23 is skipped in favor of the narrative chapters around it.
corruption_paragraphs: Not-as-bad qualifier misread. 2 Kings 17:2's phrase 'he did evil... but not as the kings of Israel that were before him' has sometimes been read as partial vindication of Hoshea — the least-bad of a bad lot. The narrative immediately undercuts this: Hoshea's nine-year reign ended in the fall of Samaria, the destruction of the northern kingdom, and the deportation of the ten tribes. The not-as-bad-as-Ahab qualifier is a bitter Chronicler-irony, not a vindication. Even diminished apostasy in the final king did not avert the long-prepared judgment that the earlier kings had earned.

Geopolitical-pressure determinism. Modern Near-Eastern-history readings of 722 BC sometimes treat the fall of Samaria as the predictable outcome of Assyrian military superiority and Israelite geopolitical miscalculation (appealing to Egypt against the wrong superpower). 2 Kings 17:7-23 explicitly rejects this reading. The 27-verse theological retrospective gives the cause as covenant breach, not military weakness: 'For so it was, that the children of Israel had sinned against the LORD their God... and walked in the statutes of the heathen... and the children of Israel did secretly those things that were not right against the LORD their God... and they served idols, whereof the LORD had said unto them, Ye shall not do this thing' (verses 7-12). Geopolitics was the instrument; covenant judgment was the cause.
roots_summary: Hebrew Hoshea (H1954) — "salvation," from yasha ("to save"). Same root as Joshua and Jesus. Nineteenth and final king of the divided northern kingdom (c. 732-722 BC); deposed when Samaria fell to Sargon II.

usage: Hoshea — "salvation"; the haunting name of the king under whom no salvation came to the northern kingdom.
Evil but not as the kings of Israel that were before him (2 Kings 17:2) — the bitter Chronicler-irony at the end.
Samaria fell to Sargon II in 722 BC; the ten tribes carried into the exile from which they never returned as a distinct people.

etymology: Hebrew Yarobam (H3379) — "may the people contend," "contender of the people," or possibly "the people will be many." From rib ("to strive, contend") + am ("people"). Named for the first king of the divided northern kingdom (Jeroboam I son of Nebat), under whom the golden-calf cult was established.
biblical_def: Jeroboam II (c. 793 — 753 BC) was the thirteenth king of the northern kingdom of Israel (2 Kings 14:23-29), great-grandson of Jehu, who reigned forty-one years — the longest reign of any king in the divided monarchy north or south — and oversaw the greatest territorial expansion and material prosperity Israel had known since the days of Solomon. He recovered the coast from Hamath in the north to the Sea of the Arabah (Dead Sea) in the south (2 Kings 14:25), restoring the boundaries of the kingdom to what Solomon had ruled. Yet the canonical verdict assigns him only seven verses in 2 Kings 14:23-29 because his prosperity coincided with the most severe spiritual decay of the northern kingdom: "He did that which was evil in the sight of the LORD: he departed not from all the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, who made Israel to sin" (2 Kings 14:24). The fuller theological commentary on his reign is delivered through the prophets who ministered during it: Amos and Hosea. Amos was sent from Tekoa in Judah to Bethel in Israel during Jeroboam II's prosperity to denounce the wealthy women of Samaria as "kine of Bashan," the merchants who falsified the ephah and made the shekel great, the rulers who sold the righteous for silver and the poor for a pair of shoes, the luxurious houses of ivory in Samaria built on injustice. Hosea, an Israelite prophet himself, called the northern kingdom adulteress, harlot-Israel, the unfaithful wife of Yahweh. Jeroboam II's reign is the great Old Testament case study in prosperous-apostasy: the kingdom was militarily expanding, economically flourishing, and spiritually rotting all at once. He died (presumably) in his bed; his son Zechariah was assassinated after six months, and the northern kingdom's final forty years (753-722 BC) were a chaotic succession of coups, civil wars, and Assyrian invasions ending in the fall of Samaria.
webster_summary: Thirteenth king of the northern kingdom of Israel (c. 793-753 BC); great-grandson of Jehu; reigned 41 years (longest of any divided-monarchy king); restored Israel's borders to Solomonic extent; reign of great prosperity and great apostasy; ministry of Amos and Hosea fell within his reign.
webster_full: JEROBOAM II, proper noun. Hebrew Yarobam (H3379) — "may the people contend," from rib ("strive") + am ("people").
Thirteenth king of the divided northern kingdom of Israel (c. 793-753 BC); great-grandson of Jehu (Jehu — Jehoahaz — Joash — Jeroboam II).
Reigned 41 years (longest of any king in either the divided-northern or divided-southern kingdom); restored Israel's borders from Hamath to the Sea of the Arabah (2 Kings 14:25).
Prophesied by the otherwise-unknown Jonah son of Amittai of Gath-hepher (2 Kings 14:25) — the same Jonah who later went to Nineveh.
Contemporary of Amos and Hosea; the great Old Testament case study in prosperous-apostasy.
scriptures: 2 Kings 14:25

He restored the coast of Israel from the entering of Hamath unto the sea of the plain, according to the word of the LORD God of Israel, which he spake by the hand of his servant Jonah, the son of Amittai, the prophet, which was of Gath-hepher.
Amos 6:1-6

Woe to them that are at ease in Zion, and trust in the mountain of Samaria... That lie upon beds of ivory, and stretch themselves upon their couches, and eat the lambs out of the flock... That drink wine in bowls, and anoint themselves with the chief ointments: but they are not grieved for the affliction of Joseph.
Hosea 4:1-2

Hear the word of the LORD, ye children of Israel: for the LORD hath a controversy with the inhabitants of the land, because there is no truth, nor mercy, nor knowledge of God in the land. By swearing, and lying, and killing, and stealing, and committing adultery, they break out, and blood toucheth blood.
I hate, I despise your feast days, and I will not smell in your solemn assemblies... But let judgment run down as waters, and righteousness as a mighty stream.
corruption_summary: Jeroboam II is corrupted when his territorial expansion and economic prosperity are treated as canonical praise (they receive only seven verses precisely because Scripture is not impressed by them), when the prophetic indictment of Amos and Hosea is read in isolation from the kingly reign that occasioned it, or when his name's connection to the founder of the golden-calf cult (Jeroboam I) is overlooked.
corruption_paragraphs: Prosperity-as-blessing misreading. Jeroboam II is sometimes presented in popular histories as a kind of Solomon-redux of the northern kingdom — an expansionist, prosperous, internationally respected king. The text refuses this framing. Seven verses in 2 Kings 14:23-29 plus the entire books of Amos and Hosea ministering against his kingdom add up to one of the longest sustained prophetic indictments in the Old Testament. The prosperity itself is part of the indictment: it was built on falsified weights (Amos 8:5), oppression of the poor (Amos 2:6-7), drunken luxury (Amos 6:4-6), and continuing high-places worship at Bethel and Dan. The doctrinal lesson: economic flourishing in a covenant-rejecting nation is a sign of judgment ripening, not blessing.

Jonah-of-Gath-hepher cameo. 2 Kings 14:25 gives the curious detail that Jeroboam II's territorial expansion fulfilled the prophecy of "Jonah, the son of Amittai, the prophet, which was of Gath-hepher" — the same Jonah of the book of Jonah. This means that the prophet who would later be sent reluctantly to Nineveh had earlier prophesied prosperity for his own apostate northern kingdom. The juxtaposition is theologically rich: Jonah was happy to prophesy national prosperity to wicked Israel but resented being sent to prophesy mercy to Nineveh. The doctrinal point is uncomfortable: prophetic gifting does not guarantee prophetic willingness to bear God's compassion to outsiders.
roots_summary: Hebrew Yarobam (H3379) — "may the people contend," from rib + am. Named for Jeroboam I, founder of the divided northern kingdom and of the golden-calf cult. Thirteenth king of Israel (c. 793-753 BC); 41-year reign.

Compound: rib ("to strive, contend") + am ("people")
Named for Jeroboam I son of Nebat, founder of the divided northern kingdom and of the golden-calf cult at Bethel and Dan
Thirteenth king of the divided northern kingdom of Israel (c. 793-753 BC); great-grandson of Jehu
41-year reign — longest of any king in either divided-monarchy kingdom; contemporary of Amos, Hosea, and Jonah
usage: Jeroboam II — the thirteenth king of the divided northern kingdom; great-grandson of Jehu; longest-reigning king of the divided monarchy.
Restored Israel's borders from Hamath to the Sea of the Arabah; the great Old Testament case study in prosperous-apostasy.
Under his reign Amos prophesied of the kine of Bashan and Hosea of the harlot-bride; both books make sense only against his prosperity.

etymology: Hebrew Basha (H1201); uncertain meaning, possibly "boldness" or "foul-smelling" (a possible derisive nickname recorded in Hebrew). Etymology is contested.
biblical_def: Baasha (c. 909 — 886 BC) was the third king of the northern kingdom of Israel (1 Kings 15:16-16:7), founder of the second dynastic line in the north (after the brief two-king Nadab line of Jeroboam I), military strongman who came to the throne by assassinating King Nadab during the siege of Gibbethon, and reigned twenty-four years from the city of Tirzah. His coup against Nadab carried out a divine sentence pronounced earlier by the prophet Ahijah the Shilonite against the house of Jeroboam I: "every male of the house of Jeroboam, that pisseth against the wall, and him that is shut up and left in Israel" (1 Kings 14:10-11) was to be cut off, and Baasha executed this judgment by killing every member of Jeroboam's family (1 Kings 15:29). Yet despite being the instrument of divine judgment against the house of Jeroboam, Baasha promptly continued in Jeroboam's golden-calf apostasy: "And he did evil in the sight of the LORD, and walked in the way of Jeroboam, and in his sin wherewith he made Israel to sin" (1 Kings 15:34). His reign was dominated by sustained low-grade warfare against the southern kingdom under King Asa of Judah, especially over the strategic border-town of Ramah (about five miles north of Jerusalem) which Baasha tried to fortify as a base for raiding Judah. Asa responded by hiring the Aramean king Ben-Hadad to attack Israel from the north (1 Kings 15:18-21); Baasha had to abandon his Ramah project; Asa took the building stones Baasha had assembled and used them to fortify the rival Judahite border-towns of Geba and Mizpah. The prophet Jehu son of Hanani then pronounced over Baasha the same kind of judgment Baasha himself had been the instrument of: his whole house would be cut off as Jeroboam's had been (1 Kings 16:1-4). Baasha died in his bed; his son Elah was assassinated in his second year by Zimri; the entire family of Baasha was extinguished in a single coup.
webster_summary: Third king of the northern kingdom of Israel (c. 909-886 BC); founder of the second northern dynasty; assassinated King Nadab; executed divine judgment against the house of Jeroboam I; reigned 24 years; continued in Jeroboam's golden-calf apostasy; warred against Asa of Judah over Ramah.
webster_full: BAASHA, proper noun. Hebrew Basha (H1201); uncertain meaning, possibly "boldness" or a derisive Hebrew form.
Third king of the divided northern kingdom of Israel (c. 909-886 BC); founder of the second northern dynasty.
Assassinated King Nadab during the siege of Gibbethon (1 Kings 15:27-28); cut off every male of the house of Jeroboam I in fulfillment of Ahijah the Shilonite's prophecy (1 Kings 15:29 / 14:10-11).
Reigned 24 years from Tirzah; warred against King Asa of Judah; tried to fortify Ramah against Judah but was driven off when Asa hired Ben-Hadad of Aram.

Verdict: 'walked in the way of Jeroboam, and in his sin wherewith he made Israel to sin' (1 Kings 15:34); prophet Jehu son of Hanani pronounced equivalent judgment over Baasha's house (1 Kings 16:1-4).
scriptures: In the third year of Asa king of Judah began Baasha the son of Ahijah to reign over all Israel in Tirzah, twenty and four years. And he did evil in the sight of the LORD, and walked in the way of Jeroboam, and in his sin wherewith he made Israel to sin.
1 Kings 15:29

And it came to pass, when [Baasha] reigned, that he smote all the house of Jeroboam; he left not to Jeroboam any that breathed, until he had destroyed him, according unto the saying of the LORD, which he spake by his servant Ahijah the Shilonite.
1 Kings 16:1-4

Then the word of the LORD came to Jehu the son of Hanani against Baasha, saying, Forasmuch as I exalted thee out of the dust, and made thee prince over my people Israel; and thou hast walked in the way of Jeroboam, and hast made my people Israel to sin, to provoke me to anger with their sins; Behold, I will take away the posterity of Baasha...
Hosea 1:4
And the LORD said unto him, Call his name Jezreel; for yet a little while, and I will avenge the blood of Jezreel upon the house of Jehu, and will cause to cease the kingdom of the house of Israel.
corruption_summary: Baasha is corrupted when his execution of divine judgment against the house of Jeroboam is read as self-justifying merit rather than as the instrumentality it actually was, when his persistent golden-calf apostasy after his coup is overlooked, or when the cyclical pattern of his rise-fall against Jeroboam's house and his own house's later destruction is treated as random political turbulence.
corruption_paragraphs: Instrument-as-merit misreading. Baasha carried out the LORD's pronounced judgment against the house of Jeroboam by killing every male of that house. Some readings have treated this as evidence of Baasha's own divine commissioning — he must have been God's chosen instrument, therefore he must have had divine approval. The text rejects this inference at every step. The prophet Jehu son of Hanani delivers a damning judgment against Baasha (1 Kings 16:1-4) precisely on the grounds that Baasha continued the very sin he had been exalted to judge: 'I exalted thee out of the dust... and thou hast walked in the way of Jeroboam.' Being the instrument of judgment did not absolve Baasha from being judged in turn.

Cyclical-coup as random politics. The pattern across 1 Kings 15-16 is striking: Jeroboam's house is judged by Baasha's coup; Baasha's house is judged by Zimri's coup; Zimri's seven-day reign is judged by Omri's coup. Modern Near-Eastern-history readings sometimes treat this as ordinary ancient-Near-Eastern political instability. The biblical narrator's framing is theological: each successive house began in coup-judgment against the prior house, continued in the same Jeroboamic golden-calf apostasy, and ended in coup-judgment delivered against itself. The pattern is doctrinal cause-and-effect, not random political instability.

usage: Baasha — the third king of the divided northern kingdom; founder of the second northern dynasty.
Instrument of judgment against the house of Jeroboam I; himself judged for continuing in the same apostasy.
His twenty-four-year reign in Tirzah, mostly preoccupied with border-warfare against Asa of Judah, frames the chaotic ninth-century political instability of the northern kingdom.
